analysis.one_liner: Stops a foreign-owned copper company from taking a sacred Arizona site.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Oak Flat land swap never got a hearing: it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and two subcommittees from March 2023 until the term ended, with 62 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2015 defense bill added a last-minute provision requiring the government to hand 2,422 acres of the Tonto National Forest called Oak Flat to Resolution Copper, a mining company jointly owned by Rio Tinto and BHP. Oak Flat is a sacred ceremonial site for Apache tribes, and the planned block-cave mine would draw down groundwater in a drought-stricken region and leave a huge waste dump in the Gila River watershed. This bill would cancel that land transfer and permanently withdraw Oak Flat from mining.
analysis.who_benefits: Tribes — above all the San Carlos Apache — for whom Oak Flat is a place of worship, since the bill repeals the transfer that would end ceremonies there. It also protects groundwater relied on by communities in Arizona's East Salt River Valley, where the bill's findings say the mine would pump roughly 250 billion gallons over 40 years and cause land subsidence, during a period when southwestern homeowners already face water restrictions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Apache tribes and Arizona water users

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals section 3003 of the 2015 defense authorization law, which mandates that Oak Flat be transferred to Resolution Copper within 60 days of an Environmental Impact Statement being published.
It also withdraws the 2,422-acre Oak Flat area from all forms of mining entry, appropriation, and mineral leasing, making the protection permanent rather than a one-time repeal.

The bill's findings document what would otherwise happen: a crater 1.8 miles long and at least 1,000 feet deep at the ceremonial site, at least 775,000 acre-feet of pumped groundwater, and a roughly 4,000-acre, 500-foot-tall toxic waste dump in the Gila River watershed.

analysis.who_pays: Resolution Copper, jointly owned by the international mining companies Rio Tinto and BHP, loses the congressionally mandated land swap and its path to one of the world's largest untapped copper deposits. Regional economies around Globe-Miami, Arizona would also forgo the construction and operating jobs a large mine would have brought, and the bill offers no replacement for that activity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Rio Tinto and BHP's Resolution Copper

drawbacks.text: Copper is central to power lines, electric vehicles, and grid storage, and Resolution would be one of the largest untapped domestic deposits, so blocking the swap removes a major potential US supply as demand climbs. The bill's answer — that the 2015 law never required the copper to be sold in the United States and that over 25 percent of US-mined copper was exported in 2022 — is only a full rebuttal if Congress also addresses where US copper goes.

The withdrawal is written 'subject to valid rights in existence' on the day of enactment, so any mining claims or property interests already perfected at Oak Flat would survive the repeal, leaving a potential gap in the protection it promises.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and hard to replace: permanent protection of a living sacred site, ceremonies that cannot be relocated, and groundwater in a region already rationing water. The costs — forgone copper supply, jobs, and investment in a project its owners had pursued for years — are real but narrow, and the bill text undercuts the strongest supply argument by showing the mine's copper was never required to stay in the country. On balance, a well-designed protection whose main cost falls on two of the world's largest mining companies.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to two of its subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the term ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on March 3, 2023, with five original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
On April 14, 2023 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources and the Subcommittee on Federal Lands, and the record shows no further action for the rest of the 118th Congress.

The bill would repeal section 3003 of the 2015 defense authorization law, which mandates the transfer of 2,422 acres of the Tonto National Forest to Resolution Copper within 60 days of publication of an Environmental Impact Statement, and would withdraw Oak Flat from all mining and mineral-leasing activity.

The bill's findings state that Resolution Copper is jointly owned by Rio Tinto and BHP, and that Rio Tinto's largest shareholder traces to a holding company under the Chinese government's state assets commission; the findings also cite Rio Tinto's 2020 destruction of the 46,000-year-old Juukan Gorge rock shelters in Australia.
Because the land-transfer mandate came from a rider attached to a must-pass defense bill over recorded congressional opposition, undoing it required a standalone vote that never occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Resolution Copper and its owners, Rio Tinto and BHP, are better off: without the repeal, the 2015 mandate to hand over Oak Flat stays on the books, and the company keeps its path to one of the world's largest copper deposits. Members of the committee majority who never scheduled a hearing also faced no vote on the issue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Resolution Copper's owners, Rio Tinto and BHP

for.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited the original cosponsors.

for.name: 62 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.

for.name: San Carlos Apache tribal members and Apache Stronghold
for.role: Tribal community campaign to protect Oak Flat
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned and litigated to stop the Oak Flat land transfer, framing the mine as destruction of their place of worship.

against.name: Rep. Bruce Westerman
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in committee and subcommittee without action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Resolution Copper (Rio Tinto and BHP)
against.role: Foreign-owned mining consortium seeking the Oak Flat land exchange
against.what_they_did: Pursued the land swap and defended the 2015 mandate that would convey Oak Flat to the company.

sides.party_line_note: All 62 cosponsors were House Democrats (62 of 216), no House Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired Natural Resources Committee never moved the bill to a hearing or vote.

industries.industry: Copper mining (Resolution Copper, owned by Rio Tinto and BHP)
industries.note: The bill repeals the congressionally mandated land swap and withdraws Oak Flat, ending the company's path to one of the world's largest untapped copper deposits. Its mine would draw roughly 250 billion gallons of groundwater over 40 years and leave a 4,000-acre waste dump, costs borne by nearby residents and tribes rather than the company.

industries.industry: Electrification and grid manufacturers that depend on copper supply
industries.note: Blocking the mine removes a major potential domestic copper source at a time of rising demand for grids and electric vehicles, though the bill notes over a quarter of US-mined copper was exported in 2022 and the 2015 law never required domestic sale, so the public gain is uncertain too.
